draft.draft_body: {"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"A man wakes up one morning and finds he has become a large insect. That is the whole setup of Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis, and it is told so plainly that you almost believe it. What matters is not the insect. What matters is what his family does next."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"They never once ask who he is now. They ask who he was, and they mourn what he can no longer do for them. That is the tragedy, and it has nothing to do with a bug."}]},{"type":"captionedImage","content":[{"type":"image2","attrs":{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/51908478-f1ab-403b-89f6-6c914f29b2dc_494x794.png","alt":"Franz Kafka, circa 1906"}},{"type":"caption","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Franz Kafka, circa 1906. Photo: Atelier Jacobi (Sigismund Jacobi). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons."}]}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The question behind the story"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The Metamorphosis reads as a story about feeling cut off, and it is. But there is an older question underneath it. Who am I, apart from my body, my job, and the parts I play? Kafka shows what it costs when those parts are torn away. A very old teaching from India, called Advaita Vedanta, shows what is left when you stop holding on to them."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"They are not the same story. They are the same question, looked at from two ends. Kafka looks at it from the dark end. The old teaching looks at it from the quiet end."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The transformation is a question, not a plot"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Gregor does not become a monster. He becomes something that no longer works. The traveling salesman, the one who brings home money, the son who pays the debts: all of it is gone in one morning. What makes it so hard to read is the way Kafka tells it, calmly, like a small inconvenience. That is exactly how a person loses their sense of who they are."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The old teaching asks the same thing. What is the self, apart from the parts it plays? Its answer is that the self is not the body and not the mind. It is the awareness that both appear inside. Gregor's trouble is what happens when the parts are taken away and the thing underneath has never been looked at."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Why his family cannot reach him"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The real sadness is not that Gregor changed. It is that his family stopped seeing him. They look at the insect and see something other, something to be rid of. The person is still in there. They just cannot see past the new shape."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The old teaching has a name for this. It calls it Maya, the power that makes the one look like many. The family cannot reach the real Gregor because they cannot see past the insect. In the same way, we cannot reach the real person in someone when we cannot see past their shape. It is not the change that is the tragedy. It is the refusal to look past it."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The job, and the one who watches"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Gregor's whole sense of himself is his work. The moment he cannot work, he stops being anybody. His family keeps him in the room while he earns, and lets him go the day he cannot. This is Kafka's clearest warning about work, and it means more now than it did in 1915. A life that tells you to keep producing does not just pay you for it. It makes you think you are the making."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The old teaching warns against exactly this. It says freedom, which it calls Moksha, comes when you see that the roles and the achievements you hold onto are not you. Kafka asks what you are when you can no longer work. The teaching answers: not the one who acts, but the one who watched it all."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The senselessness, and the way through it"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Kafka never says why the change happened. There is no reason, no cause, no fixing it. The world of the story is one in which things happen for no reason we can use. Gregor's death is as without reason as his change, and barely anyone marks it."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The old teaching does not deny that the world can feel this way. It says it feels senseless when we insist on finding a meaning inside the two sides, the good and the bad. The way through is not to explain the suffering. It is to see past the frame that makes it feel empty."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"What his death means"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Read plainly, Gregor dies alone, and the family is relieved. Read through the old teaching, the death is the letting go of the small self. The expectations, the attachments, the role he could not leave: all of it falls away. The suffering was real, and it was also the door."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The teaching says suffering that comes from not seeing clearly can become a kind of waking, if we use it to look inward. Gregor is given that chance, and he does not take it. That is the difference between the two endings. His Gregor dies without seeing through the illusion. The teaching says you do not have to."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Why this still matters"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The shapes of feeling cut off change. The feeling itself does not. We are more connected than ever, and more alone. We chase meaning in a life that moves too fast, and we let work tell us what we are worth. Kafka names the sickness: love that depends on what you do for someone. The old teaching names a way toward a different kind of love, one that does not depend on the shape you are in."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Looked at together, they say one thing. The parts you play are real, and they are not you. Kafka shows what it costs to forget that. The old teaching shows what is there when the parts fall away."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Gregor had to be peeled down to nothing to learn this. You do not have to wait to become an insect."}]}]}
